clue.text: Manacle unfastened by thriller writer

indicators.note: a manacle unfastened falls apart, so its letters are loosened and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone escapes from handcuffs with help from a writer of thrillers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfastened' is the anagram signal on MANACLE. Alistair MacLean wrote thrillers such as The Guns of Navarone.
explanation.definitionFit: Alistair MacLean was a Scottish novelist famous for wartime adventure thrillers.

clue.text: Cadfael's was Benedictine, not …

parts.note: Brother Cadfael, Ellis Peters's sleuth monk, lived in a Benedictine house at Shrewsbury; Benedictine is also a liqueur, which leads into the next clue's list of drinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Benedictine' reads as a liqueur, and the clue runs on into 2-down's list of aperitifs, but here it names Cadfael's religious order and the house he lived in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadfael was a monk of Shrewsbury Abbey, a house of Benedictine brothers.

clue.text: … "Cinzano, Bonomelli, ——' illustrious names" (A. Huxley, Antic Hay)

definitions.text: … "Cinzano, Bonomelli, ——' illustrious names" (A. Huxley, Antic Hay)

parts.words: … "Cinzano, Bonomelli, ——' illustrious names" (A. Huxley, Antic Hay)
parts.note: a gap in a quotation from Huxley's novel Antic Hay, a list of Italian drinks brands, continuing from 1-down's 'Benedictine, not'

explanation.walkthrough: Read with 1-down, the pair says the liqueur Benedictine is not one of these Italian names; the missing brand is a red bitter aperitif.
explanation.definitionFit: Campari is a famous Italian bitter aperitif, a brand name alongside Cinzano vermouth.

clue.text: The Sword in the Stone?

parts.note: T. H. White's book title, read as asking for the name of Arthur's legendary blade

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that in many tellings the sword pulled from the stone and Arthur's famous named blade are different weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend King Arthur's sword bears this name, often identified with the blade drawn from the stone.

clue.text: Freewheeling poet of the New Yorker

definitions.text: Freewheeling poet of the New Yorker

parts.words: Freewheeling poet of the New Yorker
parts.note: a light-verse writer whose loose, sprawling rhymes appeared in The New Yorker magazine

explanation.walkthrough: Ogden Nash wrote comic verse with famously free-running line lengths, published largely in The New Yorker.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogden Nash was an American humorous poet closely linked with The New Yorker.

clue.text: O'Flaherty's sort of retaliation

parts.note: points to a short-story title by the Irish writer Liam O'Flaherty, whose title names a kind of revenge

explanation.walkthrough: Liam O'Flaherty's story is 'The Pedlar's Revenge'; 'retaliation' stands for revenge, so the answer is the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The O'Flaherty story title describes revenge taken by a travelling hawker.

clue.text: Utilize yon phallic characters in a sound way

indicators.note: to utilize the letters is to put them to new use, rebuilding them into another word

explanation.surface: An instruction to make use of some rude letters for proper phonetic effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utilize' signals rearranging the ten letters of YON PHALLIC; 'characters' is a link telling you to work with them as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done by phonetic means is done in terms of speech sounds.

clue.text: Colette book has a very short time to describe cathedral

parts.note: Duo is a 1934 novel by the French writer Colette
a mo is a moment, a very short time

explanation.surface: A novel by Colette quickly describes a great church.
explanation.walkthrough: Colette's novel Duo gives the first three letters; 'mo' is British slang for a moment, as in 'half a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: Duomo is the Italian word for a cathedral church, as in Florence's.

clue.text: "To be driven round in these new horseless machines was— ——' of which we never tired" (Roy Campbell, Light on a Dark Horse)

definitions.text: "To be driven round in these new horseless machines was— ——' of which we never tired" (Roy Campbell, Light on a Dark Horse)

parts.words: "To be driven round in these new horseless machines was— ——' of which we never tired" (Roy Campbell, Light on a Dark Horse)
parts.note: a gap in Roy Campbell's memoir describing the excitement of riding in early motor cars

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from the sense: a ride in an early car was an excitement that never wore off.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing phrase means an exciting experience, which suits early motoring.

clue.text: Like the temptations of Mary Hewitt

definitions.text: Like the temptations of Mary Hewitt

parts.words: Like the temptations of Mary Hewitt
parts.note: points to the number in the title of a Victorian dramatic poem by Mary Howitt about temptations

explanation.walkthrough: Mary Howitt (printed Hewitt) wrote 'The Seven Temptations' (1834); the answer is the number in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Howitt's work counts the temptations, so they are numbered as one more than six.

clue.text: Conventional interior of casino Mickey Spillane depicted

indicators.note: the interior of a phrase is the run of letters inside it, crossing the word break

explanation.surface: A traditional scene inside a casino, as Mickey Spillane would paint it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interior of' sends you inside 'casino Mickey'; 'Spillane depicted' is surface dressing for the pulp crime writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomic is a rare word for customary or habitual, based on convention.

clue.text: Spanish nobleman's sustained speech is subdued, this Nobel prizewinner implies

definitions.text: Spanish nobleman's sustained speech is subdued, this Nobel prizewinner implies

parts.words: Spanish nobleman's sustained speech is subdued, this Nobel prizewinner implies
parts.note: paraphrases a famous novel title: a Spanish nobleman is a Don, sustained speech is a flow, subdued is quiet

explanation.walkthrough: The clue rewrites the title 'And Quiet Flows the Don', the Russian novel whose author won the 1965 Nobel Prize; the Don here is really a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Sholokhov wrote And Quiet Flows the Don and won the Nobel Prize for Literature.

clue.text: The real centre of the household, said GBS

definitions.text: The real centre of the household, said GBS

parts.words: The real centre of the household, said GBS
parts.note: recalls a line in Bernard Shaw's Heartbreak House, where horses' quarters are called the real centre of the household

explanation.walkthrough: GBS is George Bernard Shaw; in Heartbreak House a character says that in English country houses the place where horses live is the real centre of the household.
explanation.definitionFit: A building for keeping horses, which Shaw mocked as the heart of the English gentry's home.

clue.text: New intro in a very early form of shorthand

indicators.note: a new version of the letters is a fresh arrangement of them

explanation.surface: An introduction to an ancient system of rapid writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' signals rearranging INTRO IN A. Tironian notes were the shorthand of Cicero's secretary Tiro.
explanation.definitionFit: Tironian notes were a Roman system of abbreviated writing named after Cicero's freedman Tiro.

clue.text: Conviction of Janeites

definitions.meaning: belonging to Jane Austen enthusiasts, as one of Austen's novels

explanation.walkthrough: Janeites are Jane Austen devotees; 'Conviction' looks legal but means a belief.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm belief is a persuasion; Janeites, devoted fans of Austen, revere her final completed novel of that name.

clue.text: Lamb the Second? (His anger was kindled against David)

definitions.text: His anger was kindled against David

parts.note: Charles Lamb wrote his essays under the pen name Elia
B is the second letter, as in a B grade for second class

explanation.surface: A question about a second Lamb, with a note about a man's fury at David.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is the essayist Charles Lamb, not a sheep. In 1 Samuel 17:28 David's eldest brother is angry with him on the battlefield against Goliath.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliab, David's eldest brother, scolded him for coming to watch the battle, as the Bible records.

clue.text: "I will talk of things moral, or things — al" (Bunyan)

definitions.text: "I will talk of things moral, or things — al" (Bunyan)

parts.words: "I will talk of things moral, or things — al" (Bunyan)
parts.note: a gap in Talkative's speech in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, where the missing word stem precedes the ending 'al'

explanation.walkthrough: Talkative in The Pilgrim's Progress offers to discuss things moral or things concerning the gospel; the answer plus 'al' completes the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The stem means relating to the Christian gospel, set beside moral matters in the quotation.

clue.text: Fête with new saint for Pauline addressees

parts.note: a fête is a festive occasion, a gala

indicators.note: a new form of the word saint is a fresh arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A celebration with a newly canonised saint, for people St Paul wrote to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' signals rearranging SAINT into TIANS. Paul's Epistle to the Galatians is a New Testament book.
explanation.definitionFit: The Galatians were the churches of Galatia who received one of St Paul's letters.

clue.text: Like public transport with Morgan

parts.note: points to a story title by E. M. Forster, whose middle name was Morgan, about a heavenly bus

explanation.walkthrough: Morgan is Edward Morgan Forster, not a car maker; his story 'The Celestial Omnibus' has a bus that runs to heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's omnibus is heavenly, so the bus is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Ancestral Christmas tree, a present from Norway

definitions.text: Ancestral Christmas tree, a present from Norway

parts.words: Ancestral Christmas tree, a present from Norway
parts.note: plays on Norway's annual gift of a Christmas tree to London, pointing instead to the great tree of Norse myth

explanation.walkthrough: Norway sends a Christmas tree to Trafalgar Square each year; the 'ancestral' Norse tree is the ash that holds the worlds together.
explanation.definitionFit: Yggdrasil is the immense world ash of Norse mythology, linking heaven, earth and the underworld.

clue.text: Quasi archangel with warning for whalers

definitions.text: Quasi archangel with warning for whalers

parts.words: Quasi archangel with warning for whalers
parts.note: points to the mad prophet aboard the Jeroboam in Moby-Dick who shares an archangel's name and warns against hunting the white whale

explanation.walkthrough: In Melville's Moby-Dick the crazed Shaker on the Jeroboam claims to be the archangel whose name he bears and warns Ahab off the whale.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moby-Dick prophet shares his name with the messenger angel of the Annunciation.

clue.text: Some, or nearly all, of light novelist

indicators.note: some of the phrase means only part of its letters are taken, a run inside it

explanation.surface: A popular novelist appears in some or most of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some ... of' sends you inside 'nearly all'. Edna Lyall was a popular Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Edna Lyall was the pen name of a Victorian author of popular romantic fiction.

clue.text: Poor caviare exhibited by Moliere protagonist

indicators.note: poor caviare is spoilt caviare, so its letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Second-rate caviar served up by a Molière hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' signals rearranging CAVIARE. Molière's L'Avare (The Miser) centres on the hoarding Harpagon.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed for money is the vice of Harpagon, Molière's miser.

clue.text: Emperor, say, of seat of the Sanhedrin

indicators.note: say points to a word spoken, here the emperor's name as it is pronounced

parts.note: Tiberius was the second Roman emperor

explanation.surface: Asking which emperor, for instance, is linked with the Jewish council's seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks a sound-alike of the emperor Tiberius; the Galilee city was named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiberias in Galilee became the last seat of the Jewish council after the Roman wars.

clue.text: Topic from The Lives of the Medicis

indicators.note: the letters are taken from inside the words, running across the word break

explanation.surface: A subject drawn from a history of the Medici family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' sends you inside 'the Medicis'; 'The Lives of' is title dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the subject a piece of writing or talk is about.

clue.text: Flanders rose of Meredith?

parts.note: Meredith's novel title pairs a girl's name meaning rose in Greek with a surname meaning someone from Flanders

explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's novel is Rhoda Fleming: Fleming means a native of Flanders, and the Greek rhodon is a rose.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Meredith's Rhoda Fleming bears a name from the Greek for the flower.

clue.text: Arts backing American composer

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word arts is read from right to left

parts.note: US is the abbreviation for United States, American

explanation.surface: The arts support an American who writes music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns ARTS into STRA. Oscar Straus wrote the operetta The Chocolate Soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Straus was a Viennese operetta writer who later worked in America.

clue.text: 4 thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one

definitions.text: 4 thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one

parts.words: 4 thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one
parts.note: the 4 refers to the poet at 4-down, whose verse 'England Expects' says the English think they belong to the most exclusive society

explanation.walkthrough: Ogden Nash's 'England Expects' jokes that the English feel they belong to the most exclusive society there is.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclusive club is a select association, the image Nash used for being English.

clue.text: Journalistic leader, perhaps

parts.note: reads as a chief editor, but a leader is also the newspaper's own opinion article

explanation.walkthrough: In British papers a 'leader' is the opinion column, not a person running the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article stating its own opinion is called a leader in Britain.

clue.text: Friends of Italian astronomer and natural philosopher

definitions.meaning: Giovanni Battista ..., the Italian astronomer and microscope maker

explanation.walkthrough: Giovanni Battista Amici (1786-1863) built microscopes and telescopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Amici is Italian for pals, and also the surname of the nineteenth-century Italian optician and stargazer.

clue.text: Measure novelist as biographer

parts.note: an ell is an old measure of cloth length
Thomas Mann was the German novelist of The Magic Mountain

explanation.surface: Judging a novelist in the role of a life-writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Ellmann wrote celebrated lives of Joyce and Wilde.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Ellmann was an American scholar known for his lives of James Joyce and Oscar Wilde.

clue.text: Not in fact biography of a biographer by Stanley Elkin

definitions.text: Not in fact biography of a biographer by Stanley Elkin

parts.words: Not in fact biography of a biographer by Stanley Elkin
parts.note: Stanley Elkin's first novel bears the name of Johnson's famous biographer but is fiction, not a life of him

explanation.walkthrough: Elkin's 1964 novel shares its title with Samuel Johnson's biographer, but it is a comic fiction about a modern man.
explanation.definitionFit: James Boswell wrote the Life of Johnson; Elkin borrowed the surname for his novel.
